Content covers: the beraita permitting a donkey to be led out alongside the heifer per the first Tanna (l01a); the derivation, from 'and Elazar the priest shall take of its blood,' that the receiving and sprinkling of the heifer's blood are performed specifically by Elazar, with Shmuel's and Rav's differing accounts of why the verse needed to state this given the surrounding restriction-after-restriction structure (l04); the further derivation that the casting of the cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool likewise requires a priest (though not necessarily Elazar specifically), again with Shmuel's and Rav's differing analyses of which implications are self-standing versus exclusionary (l07); the requirement that the priest wash his garments 'in his priesthood,' teaching that the whole procedure must be performed in priestly garments even for future generations (l11); the question of how this squares with the view that future-generation performance uses an ordinary priest rather specifically the High Priest (l13); the derivation from 'a man' (rather than 'priest') that a non-priest is valid for gathering the ash, extended in the next clause to validate a woman as well (l17); the requirement to place water on the ash specifically in an earthenware vessel for the sanctification (l21); the beraita establishing that whoever the earlier gathering-stage verse validates or disqualifies (non-priest and woman valid; deaf-mute, imbecile, minor invalid) carries over to the taking-for-the-impure-person stage via the shared word 'they shall take' (l24); the challenge and the Rabbis' resolution of why the verse uses plural 'they shall take' rather than singular, addressing whether one or two people may jointly perform the act (l28, l30); and the extended analysis of the sanctification-stage verse 'and a pure man shall take hyssop,' including the Rabbis' and Rabbi Yehuda's opposing readings of whether 'man' and 'pure' independently validate or exclude a woman versus a minor (l35).
